The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: US ties Chinese satellite imagery to strike that killed three troops
brief.h: American officials say Tehran obtained high-resolution imagery of Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base from Chinese suppliers both before and after the 17 July ballistic-missile strike that killed three US soldiers, but have not named the firms and have stopped short of accusing Beijing of directing it.
brief.t: The important thing here is not a satellite - it is that commercial geospatial imagery has become a belligerent input a state can supply without supplying a single weapon. Call it the arms-length arsenal: a firm sells sub-metre pictures on an open platform, a customer builds a target folder from them, and the supplying government keeps a clean denial because the transaction was, in its own words, routine market practice. The pattern is already documented. In April the Defense Intelligence Agency alleged Iran's Revolutionary Guards used AI-enhanced imagery from the Chinese firm MizarVision, which published Patriot battery positions at Prince Sultan air base on 24 February and aircraft deployments on 27 February, days before Iranian missiles hit that base and killed an American. What is new tonight is lethality attached to a named event rather than a capability described in general terms.
brief.context: The rail predates the headline, which is why this reads as policy rather than accident. Washington sanctioned three China-based imagery firms in May 2026 over exactly this conduct, and Planet Labs was asked by the US government to withhold conflict-region imagery indefinitely - a government rationing its own commercial pictures is telling you it treats the product as ordnance. The deciding desk is therefore Treasury's OFAC and Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, not the Pentagon: the base rate on intelligence-support attributions is designation, entity-listing and licence denial, because a kinetic answer to a data vendor has no proportionate target. Beijing's foreign ministry has answered consistently that the imagery came from open-source channels and denies malicious intent, and this time demanded evidence. The read changes if Washington names the suppliers in a public designation tied to the Jordan strike - that converts an anonymous briefing into an enforceable instrument - or if it formally alleges state direction, which is a far larger claim than commercial supply.

angles.effect: Gain a documented predicate for the next round of export controls and designations, timed while Chinese participation in the war is the live question.
Pays reputationally but keeps the deniability the commercial structure was built to provide, and can demand evidence Washington may not want to show.
Carry the real cost - the precedent turns open satellite catalogues into licensable munitions, and Planet Labs has already been asked to go dark over the theatre.
Loses little; the imagery has already been used, and targeting knowledge does not expire when a supplier is sanctioned.

dec.kill: A public Treasury or Commerce designation naming the specific suppliers and citing the Jordan strike would move this from anonymous attribution to instrument. Conversely, a US finding that the imagery reached Iran through resellers without the vendors' knowledge would collapse the deliberate-supply read.

brief.head: Iraq seals its Iran border crossing and hunts the drone crews
brief.h: Two security sources say Baghdad ordered the Shalamcheh crossing with Iran shut as a precaution and launched a wide-scale operation to find those behind the drone strikes on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, a day after sacking the commander of its Maysan Operations Command.
brief.t: Closing a border crossing is the cheapest visible act a government can perform, which is precisely why Baghdad performed it. The currency being bought is time: Riyadh named a state rather than a militia, said it would not respond at this stage, and is waiting to see whether Iraq's sovereignty theatre converts into real control of the launch environment in its own south. Follow the physical ledger underneath the diplomacy and the picture is harsher than the statements - Saudi crude output fell by 2.3 million barrels a day in August to roughly 6 million, the lowest in more than three decades, and Reuters reports the crown prince called President Trump twice on Thursday asking for military assistance. Monday's meeting in Oman with Iraq and Gulf states on Hormuz shipping safety is the real venue; the border gate is the press release.
brief.context: Petroline exists because of this exact scenario - it was built in the 1980s so Saudi barrels could reach the Red Sea without passing Iran's guns at Hormuz, and a bypass that is itself in range from Iraqi territory is not a bypass, it is a second front. The rail that decides is not the crossing but the loading programme: Aramco's October nominations for Yanbu, published at normal volumes or not at all, separate a routing interruption from a production loss, and they outrank every statement either government makes this week. The base rate is not encouraging. Iraqi governments have dismissed regional commanders after cross-border attacks before without stopping the next launch, because the factions operating these systems answer to a patronage structure rather than to the operations command that gets sacked. What would change the read is a second launch from Iraqi soil - that single event settles whether the Maysan dismissal bought control or only a delay, and it is the phrase 'at this stage' that then has to cash.

angles.effect: Buys deniability and time with two reversible acts - a closed gate and a sacked officer - without confronting the armed factions that actually hold the ground.
Gains a face-saving reason to defer retaliation it can hardly afford while output sits at a thirty-year low and its Red Sea exit is contested.
Pay immediately and entirely - Shalamcheh is a commercial and pilgrimage artery, and it is the civilian traffic that stops, not the drones.
Pay nothing yet. No arrests have been announced, and a 'wide-scale operation' sourced to two anonymous security officials is an intention, not a result.

dec.kill: A second drone launch from Iraqi territory kills the control story outright. An Aramco October Yanbu programme at normal volumes, or announced arrests with named units, would show the de-escalation ladder is real.

consp.claim: That the 'drones launched from Iraq' attribution is a manufactured pretext - that the strike on Petroline was not an Iraqi militia operation at all and the Iraq framing exists to license a move against Baghdad. Running alongside it, in separate all-caps threads, is the claim that the damage is being deliberately understated and that Saudi exports have in fact dropped to zero with 70 per cent of the kingdom's oil now off world markets.
consp.spread: Multiple simultaneous /pol/ happening threads, the loudest in all-caps, plus the running Persia-Israel general which is tracking Ansar Allah strikes on Abha, Khamis Mushait and Taif day by day.
consp.read: Two different claims are riding together and they deserve different answers. The pretext framing is the standard casus-belli-manufacture template applied to an attribution that was genuinely single-sourced at first - but Baghdad's own investigation confirmed the launches came from Iraqi soil and it sacked a commander over it, which is a costly admission no government volunteers to serve another state's pretext. The export-collapse numbers are wrong in a checkable way: Petroline is a bypass line of roughly 5 million barrels a day of capacity against output near 6 million, and the kingdom's principal Gulf-side terminal at Ras Tanura is not on it.

brief.head: Putin says European troops in Ukraine would mean war with Russia
brief.h: The Russian president said European leaders 'are considering how to send troops onto Ukrainian territory - that means a war against Russia', while insisting Moscow poses no threat to Europe and that the danger European governments describe 'does not exist and has never existed'.
brief.t: Read the audience, not the adjective. This threat is not aimed at Kyiv, which has no say in whether a European force deploys, and it is not aimed at the Kremlin's own hardliners, who need no convincing. It is aimed at the parliaments and finance ministries that would have to vote a mandate, fund a rotation and one day explain a casualty - and its job is to make the first boot-print politically unpayable before anyone has to decide. Notice the pairing inside a single statement: a war threat and a reassurance that Russia has no intention of threatening Europe. That is not incoherence, it is targeting. The threat goes to the governments, the reassurance goes to their voters, and the gap between the two is the strategy.
brief.context: The rail here is a promise that has never been cashed. A European reassurance force has been discussed since spring 2025, with Emmanuel Macron claiming last September that 26 of Ukraine's allies had committed to a presence on the ground, at sea or in the air once fighting ends - and it has been re-announced at leaders' meetings since without a framework nation ever publishing force numbers, a mandate or a date. The deciding desks are national: force-generation conferences in European defence ministries and the legislatures that must authorise deployment, not the summit communique. That is the base rate to hold - the announcement rate on this force runs about one a quarter and the deployment rate is zero - and it is why Putin can threaten it cheaply. What would change the read is boringly documentary: a named lead nation, published troop numbers, a parliamentary mandate vote scheduled. Absent those, this is a veto exercised over a force that does not exist.

angles.effect: Gains a free veto - it deters a deployment that was not imminent, and can claim credit for preventing it whenever the plan slips again.
Gain cover for continued deferral; a Russian war threat is a more comfortable explanation for not deploying than force-generation arithmetic and a missing mandate.
Pays in guarantee credibility - the security assurance it is being offered is the one an adversary can talk out of existence before it is written down.
Is told simultaneously that Europe is preparing war and that no threat exists, which is what a leadership says when it wants mobilised sentiment without mobilisation.

dec.kill: A framework nation publishing force numbers and a deployment date, or a national parliament scheduling a mandate vote, would turn the reassurance force into a real object and make this threat a response rather than a pre-emption.

consp.claim: That the whole war is theatre for European publics, with anons pointing at Europe still buying Russian gas as the proof - 'Russia is going to kill us, and we will keep paying them so they can'. Circulating beside it is a widely shared claim that Putin has expelled the Rothschild family from Russia outright and that they are now forbidden from setting foot on Russian territory under any circumstances.
consp.spread: A gas-purchase thread citing a Euronews report, plus a high-reply thread built on an amg-news aggregator item, both running alongside the permanent Ukraine generals which now give flatly contradictory accounts of the same front near Lyman.
consp.read: The first maps onto the 'both sides are the same management' frame and has a real kernel - European energy payments to Russia genuinely continued long past the sanctions rhetoric - but that is a policy failure under price and industrial pressure, a different object from a staged war. The second is a recurring fabrication: amg-news generates financial-cabal stories on a schedule, and the structural tell is that no decree number, ministry or legal instrument is ever cited, only the assertion that one exists.

brief.head: Congo's Ebola outbreak crosses the country and passes 7,000 cases
brief.h: Health authorities confirmed a case in Sud-Ubangi in the north-west - the seventh province affected and the first in western Congo - in a man who travelled through South Kivu, Rwanda, Uganda, Ituri and several north-eastern provinces in under three weeks, as the toll passed 7,000 infections and roughly 3,400 deaths since 15 May.
brief.t: The case count is not the news. The itinerary is. A 23-year-old man reached Gwaka in Sud-Ubangi, where he died on Tuesday with fever and vomiting blood, after a journey that crossed two international borders and most of a country the size of western Europe - which means this outbreak has stopped being an eastern emergency contained by distance and started moving along the road and river corridors that end at Kinshasa. The fatality rate sits near 48 per cent, Ituri still holds about four fifths of confirmed cases, and the WHO says the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to pass the 2014-16 West African epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people. This is already the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, it has been running since May, and it has held almost none of the world's attention.
brief.context: The constraint is not medical, it is territorial. Ebola is stopped by contact tracing and ring vaccination, both of which require reaching every contact of every case within days - and the epicentre sits in provinces where armed groups control access and health teams have been attacked before. That is why the tool that works in a stable state fails here, and why this outbreak has already doubled the size of every previous Congolese event, which typically burned out in the low thousands. The deciding bodies are the WHO's emergency machinery and the Congolese health ministry's vaccination teams working with Africa CDC, not a donor summit. The two observables that matter now point opposite ways: a confirmed case in Kinshasa province would mean the corridor thesis is right and the response has lost the geography, while 42 days - two incubation periods - with no new case in a province is the only thing that has ever ended one of these.

consp.claim: That the outbreak is not a natural event at all. The versions in circulation include that it is a political fabrication commissioned by the Congolese presidency, that aid organisations imported the disease to unlock funding, that a simple cure exists and is being withheld, and that the virus is an engineered bioweapon.
consp.spread: Heaviest in French-language TikTok video and in rumour networks inside the affected provinces, circulating since May and documented in mainstream reporting on the outbreak's information environment rather than confined to the anglophone boards.
consp.read: This maps onto the standard health-disinformation playbook, and the artificial-origin variant specifically follows a template run against HIV, Ebola and COVID for decades. The kernel that is real and measurable is the consequence rather than the claim: documented vaccine refusal in Ituri and Kivu, driven by fear that the vaccine activates other illness, directly slows ring vaccination - so the rumour is an input to the case curve, not commentary on it.

brief.head: CIA releases pre-9/11 bin Laden briefings on the 25th anniversary
brief.h: Director John Ratcliffe called the release of dozens of presidential daily briefs dated between February 1998 and 12 September 2001 'an act of exceptional transparency'; they carry hijacking, dirty-bomb and aircraft-as-weapon warnings but, on first reading, add no new detail about the plot itself, and names and identifying information stay redacted.
brief.t: A declassification released on an anniversary is an instrument with a date attached, and the date is the part the agency controls. What the briefs document is the finding the 9/11 Commission already made, and it is worth restating precisely: the system had the threat and not the target. A September 1998 brief records that the preferred option was to strike the United States on its own soil in Washington and that the network might fly an explosive-packed aircraft into a US city; a December 1998 brief notes that some members had received hijack training. That is warning - it is not warning of this, on this day, with these flights. The distance between those two sentences is the entire intelligence-failure literature, and publishing on the 25th anniversary guarantees the distinction gets collapsed by everyone reading the headline rather than the paper.
brief.context: The presidential daily brief is the most jealously protected document class in the executive branch, precisely because presidents want candour from analysts who know they will not be published - so every release is discretionary, and every release is therefore a choice about timing. The base rate to hold is the 2016 declassification of the 28 pages on Saudi links: it moved litigation far more than it moved history, feeding the families' suit against Saudi Arabia rather than rewriting the account of the attacks. Expect the same shape here - the operative consequence is discovery pressure and follow-on FOIA, not a revised narrative. The deciding desk is the CIA's historical review machinery with the DNI, not Congress, which tells you this is institutional interest rather than legislative pressure. What would change the read is a brief containing operational detail the Commission did not have, or a document withheld in full rather than redacted; the second is usually more informative than the first.

angles.effect: Gains a transparency headline on a date of its own choosing, using documents that largely confirm the existing official account rather than complicate it.
Genuinely gain - three and a half years of contemporaneous threat reporting at the highest classification is a real archive, whatever the motive for releasing it.
Gains leverage; every named liaison relationship and every redaction becomes a discovery target, which is how the 28 pages actually mattered.
Pays nothing. Names and identifying information remain concealed, and transparency measured in pages released is not transparency measured in pages unredacted.

dec.kill: A released brief carrying specific operational detail about the plot - the flights, the date, the cell - would flip this from anniversary theatre to genuine disclosure. A published index showing documents withheld in full would prove the opposite.

consp.claim: That this release is the admission - that 'they knew' is now in the government's own paper and the rest follows, with the anniversary timing read as a limited hangout designed to absorb the question rather than answer it. The threads running hardest beside it are the WTC7 reading anchored on Barry Jennings, the building's deputy director of emergency services, who described hearing explosions inside before the towers fell; the molten-steel argument that no office fire leaves metal running at Ground Zero weeks later; a thread noting Howard Lutnick survived because he took his child to school for the first time that morning; and a thread treating a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles episode showing the Technodrome crashing through New York, aired on the anniversary itself, as predictive programming.
consp.spread: Very loud - a dozen simultaneous /pol/ anniversary threads plus a dedicated predictive-programming thread on /x/, and mainstream reporting this week noted archive 9/11 footage reaching new audiences on X and Instagram and reviving the old claims with it.
consp.read: The foreknowledge frame has the real kernel and the release genuinely feeds it: the briefs do show sustained strategic warning, which is exactly why the distinction between strategic and tactical warning has to be made out loud rather than assumed. The demolition mechanics do not survive the NIST reports, and the Lutnick and cartoon items are survivorship and coincidence-mining - in a city of eight million on a weekday morning, thousands of people missed those buildings by an ordinary accident of routine. Note separately that ethnic-scapegoat versions of the anniversary narrative are circulating in volume on the same boards and on large podcasts, in mutually exclusive variants with identical structure; the persuasion technique is constant - substitute a group for a mechanism, so a question about which desk failed becomes a question about identity and stops being checkable.

watch: An Aramco October loading programme for Yanbu, at normal volumes or not at all. With the ministry having confirmed the valve is shut, this is still the only document that separates a routing interruption from a production loss, and it outranks every statement either government makes.

Monday's meeting in Oman with Iraq and Gulf states on Hormuz shipping safety. Watch whether it produces a named administrator, a fee schedule or an escort arrangement - a toll regime always announces itself as a safety mechanism.

Whether Treasury or Commerce names the Chinese imagery suppliers in a public designation tied to the Jordan strike. An anonymous attribution becomes an instrument the day a firm appears on a list, and that is the escalation channel most likely to be used.

The BRICS Delhi declaration, read for an INSTRUMENT rather than an aspiration - a named operator, a dated launch, a settlement volume. Every summit since 2009 has produced the aspiration; almost none has produced the instrument.

A confirmed Ebola case in Kinshasa province. That single datum would mean the corridor thesis is right and the response has lost the geography; conversely, any province reaching 42 days with no new case is the only thing that has ever ended one of these.
lesson: Today's lesson is the Sound Dues, and it explains why oil got CHEAPER on the day two chokepoints closed. From 1429 until 1857, Denmark charged every merchant ship passing through the Oresund - the narrow water between Denmark and Sweden - a toll simply for being allowed through. At its height the Sound Dues funded up to two-thirds of the Danish crown's revenue, and the crucial detail is that Denmark did not want to stop the ships. A blockade earns nothing. A toll earns forever, and it earns most when trade is heaviest, which gives the toll-keeper a direct financial interest in keeping the water open and merely expensive. The mechanism is worth a name: a chokepoint holder who builds an administration - a permit office, a fee schedule, an inspection regime - has revealed that they are pricing access, not denying it. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority is a permit office with a fee schedule. What it predicts now is specific and testable: expect arrangements, corridors and toll structures rather than closure, expect the holder to fight hardest over who ADMINISTERS the passage rather than whether it opens, and expect prices to settle at a plateau above the old level rather than spiking to a shortage. That is exactly what our ledger says - a 76 per cent chance any Hormuz deal preserves Iranian transit machinery, against 10 per cent that traffic actually recovers. And the honest counter-case, because the Sound Dues also show how this ends: Denmark's toll was finally bought out in 1857 by a coalition of states that paid a lump sum rather than keep paying forever. Watch for someone offering Tehran the lump sum.

events.label: Perim (Bab el-Mandeb)
events.note: Houthi forces hold the island splitting the strait at its narrowest point, completing control of Yemen's western coast. The airstrip on it is the emplacement tripwire - a capture is not a closure.

events.label: Yanbu
events.note: Red Sea terminus of the shut East-West Pipeline, and the crude source for roughly 650,000 b/d of distillate-heavy refining. An October Aramco loading programme, or its absence, is the document that settles the story.

events.label: Abqaiq
events.note: Eastern-province origin of Petroline, which was laid in 1981 precisely so Saudi crude could reach the Red Sea without passing Hormuz. That forty-five-year-old hedge is currently offline.

events.label: Maysan, Iraq
events.note: Baghdad's own investigation placed the drone launches here and dismissed the Operations Command chief. A second launch from Iraqi soil is the wire that turns a launch pad into a front.

events.label: Strait of Hormuz
events.note: Transits still in single digits a day against a pre-war baseline near 130. Gulf ministers meet Iran at Salalah on 14 September; an announcement is not a transit.

events.label: Mocha
events.note: The Red Sea port fell on 10 September, the day before Perim. The UN reports at least 46,000 people displaced along the coast in a week.

events.label: New Delhi
events.note: The 18th BRICS summit, 12-13 September, with Xi in India for the first time in nearly seven years. Watch for a named instrument rather than an aspiration.

events.label: Wonsan
events.note: Several short-range ballistic missiles fired toward the East Sea the morning after the Freedom Edge trilateral exercise ended. Seoul convened an emergency security review.

events.label: Washington
events.note: The FOMC meets 16 September. The question is not the rate but whether the statement keeps looking through energy prices after August CPI.

events.label: Putumayo
events.note: A seven-day drone spraying pilot over roughly 1,000 hectares of coca - the first aerial eradication since 2015, and the object of a new ledger question about whether a court stops it.

events.label: El Fasher, Darfur
events.note: The only geography the UN arms embargo actually covers, in a war fought nationwide. The regime was rolled over by a single month to 9 October.

events.label: Saratov
events.note: Ukrainian drone strikes on refining continue. Russia's gasoline export suspension, imposed 27 August, runs to 30 September.

fired: GEO-032 RESOLVED YES - and it resolved AGAINST US. Brier 0.314, the worst score on this ledger, against GEO-009's 0.029; two resolutions scored, mean Brier 0.171. quiz.q: Why does today's brief argue that shutting the East-West Pipeline is a DIESEL story as much as a crude story?
options: Because the pipeline carries refined diesel directly to European buyers
Because its terminus at Yanbu also supplies the crude charge for roughly 650,000 b/d of distillate-heavy refining, which cannot run without it
Because diesel is priced off pipeline tariffs rather than off crude
Because Saudi Arabia imports its diesel through the same pipeline in reverse
quiz.why: A refinery is a machine that needs a crude feed. Cutting the feed removes the products, not just the barrels - which is why the desk moved its diesel-crack question DOWN, away from the threshold, rather than up.

quiz.q: Oil prices FELL on the day a chokepoint was captured and a major bypass pipeline was shut. What does the brief say that pattern reveals?
options: That the reporting was exaggerated and little actually happened
That traders expect OPEC+ to release spare capacity immediately
That the market is pricing a higher cost of passage - a toll - rather than a physical shortage of oil
That oil markets no longer respond to Middle East events
quiz.why: A toll makes oil more expensive to move; a shortage makes it impossible to get. Prices that rise to a plateau and then fade on escalation are the signature of the first. In the staged template this is Stage A/B behaviour, not the Stage C shortage spike.

quiz.q: The new Colombia question asks whether a COURT will halt the spraying programme, not whether Colombia will spray. Why did the desk frame it that way?
options: Because courts are easier to forecast than governments
Because pricing an event that has effectively already happened is what produced today's worst-ever Brier score on the Saudi pipeline question
Because Colombian courts have never ruled on this issue before
Because US decertification legally requires judicial review in Colombia

quiz.q: What is the analytical point of the Sound Dues, the toll Denmark charged ships passing the Oresund from 1429 to 1857?
options: That naval blockades reliably force political concessions
That narrow waters are impossible to defend without a large fleet
That a chokepoint holder who builds a permit office and a fee schedule is pricing access, not denying it - and therefore wants the water open but expensive
That international law has always guaranteed freedom of navigation
quiz.why: A blockade earns nothing; a toll earns forever, and earns most when trade is heaviest. That is why the desk expects corridors and fee structures out of the Hormuz talks rather than either closure or free transit - and why 76 per cent of the probability sits on any deal preserving Iranian administration of the passage.

quiz.q: A circulating claim says BRICS Pay is 'the operational start of the dollar's collapse'. Which observable would best test it?
options: The number of heads of state who attend the Delhi summit
Whether the summit declaration uses the phrase 'local currency trade'
Whether a physical commodity cargo is settled end to end through the rail in a non-dollar unit, with volumes published
Whether the US publicly criticises the initiative
quiz.why: Attendance, rhetoric and American irritation are all cheap and all present at every summit since 2009. A settled cargo with disclosed volumes is the one thing that cannot be produced by a communique - which is why it is the falsifier and the others are noise.

That bargain traded American security guarantees for dollar-priced oil, and its unstated assumption was that the guarantor would keep the sea lanes open and would show up when a client was attacked. Both halves of that assumption were tested in one day: a chokepoint changed hands, a fire burned over the only pipeline that routes around the other chokepoint, and the guarantor declined a treaty partner's direct request for strikes, offering intelligence and targeting data instead. The old rail: a security guarantee underwritten by a navy with forward basing. The new permit: the guarantee is now explicitly partial - freedom of navigation for the lane, but the land war behind it is the partner's problem - and that repricing is happening at the same moment the monetary half of the bargain is being asked to absorb a supply shock with a demand instrument.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
